subtype: Labelled weak and living down to it [Receiver]
passage: In the one-room school outside Bhilwara, Usha Ma'am once said, "Vishal is weak at maths, let him copy from the board." She didn't say it again. She didn't need to. When she asked questions, her eyes moved past Vishal to the front row. If he started to answer, she waited only a moment before turning to someone else. Nobody asked him to come to the board anymore. By winter, Vishal kept his hand in his lap even when he knew the answer. He counted his father's goat money correctly every evening at home, but at school he left the sums blank. "I am weak," he told his little sister when she asked for help.

qa.q: What did Vishal count correctly every evening at home?
qa.a: His father's goat money.

qa.q: Why did Vishal keep his hand in his lap even when he knew the answer?
qa.a: After being called weak and passed over again and again, he felt discouraged and came to believe he was bad at maths, so trying seemed pointless.

qa.q: What could Usha Ma'am change in how she asks questions?
qa.a: She could wait as long for Vishal as for the front row and invite him to the board again, showing she expects him to be able to answer.

qa.q: How might Vishal's little sister be affected when he says "I am weak"?
qa.a: She loses a helper, and she may learn from her brother that a label means you stop trying. 😔

grounding: A village boy labelled weak at maths gets less waiting time and fewer questions, stops raising his hand and begins to live down to the label.

subtype: Labelled weak and living down to it [Receiver]
passage: In Abebe's school in Toronto, the maths groups had animal names, but everyone knew the Turtles were the slow ones. Abebe had been a Turtle since he arrived from Addis Ababa. Ms. Yara was kind, but when she asked a hard question, she looked at the Eagles table. When Abebe raised his hand, she'd say, "Let's give someone else a turn," and move on quickly. By spring, he had stopped raising it. On a quiz he froze at a fractions question he had done at home with his uncle, and wrote nothing. "Turtles don't do fractions," he mumbled to his friend. At home that night, he solved the same question in two minutes.

qa.q: Which table did Ms. Yara look at when she asked a hard question?
qa.a: The Eagles table.

qa.q: What does Abebe mumbling "Turtles don't do fractions" show about what he now believes?
qa.a: He has taken the group label as the truth about himself, so he freezes at school even though he can solve fractions at home.

qa.q: What small change could Ms. Yara make that might break this pattern?
qa.a: She could ask the Turtles hard questions too and wait for their answers, showing Abebe she expects him to handle them.

qa.q: What might Abebe's uncle think if he saw the blank quiz?
qa.a: His uncle, who worked through fractions with him at home, might be puzzled and sad, knowing Abebe can do them, and wonder what is happening at school.

grounding: A boy placed in the slow maths group gets fewer chances to answer, stops trying and freezes on work he can actually do.

subtype: Labelled weak and living down to it [Receiver]
passage: At the evening tuition centre, Deepak Sir divided the room without saying so. The front benches got the tricky word problems and long, patient explanations. Vikas had sat at the back since the first test, when Sir laughed, "Maths is not your cup of tea, Vikas." Now, if Vikas was the only hand up, Sir answered the question himself. Vikas noticed. He started drawing cars in his margin during the problems. When his mother asked about tuition, he shrugged. "I'm just bad at it. Sir knows." Last week a new student sat beside him and asked for help with a division sum. Vikas explained it perfectly, then went quiet, surprised at himself.

qa.q: What did Sir say to Vikas after the first test?
qa.a: "Maths is not your cup of tea, Vikas."

qa.q: Why did Vikas go quiet after explaining the division sum perfectly?
qa.a: He had come to believe he was bad at maths from Sir's words and cues, so doing it well surprised him and didn't fit the label.

qa.q: What could Vikas's mother do after hearing "I'm just bad at it. Sir knows"?
qa.a: She could ask him to show her a sum, notice what he can do, and talk calmly with Sir about giving Vikas the same problems and explanations as the front benches.

qa.q: How might the new student see Vikas?
qa.a: To the new student, Vikas is simply the classmate who explained division clearly, not someone who is bad at maths; the label hasn't reached them.

grounding: A boy told maths is not for him gets fewer chances at tuition, stops trying and believes the label, until helping a classmate surprises him.

subtype: Labelled weak and living down to it [Receiver]
passage: I'm Trisha, and I sit behind Deepika in Class 5. In June, after the first maths test, Ma'am read out marks and said, 'Deepika, you're weak in maths, beta. Just focus on neatness.' Ma'am never said it again. But I noticed things. When Ma'am asked tables, she went round the room and skipped Deepika. If Deepika started to answer, Ma'am said 'Hmm, anyone else?' after one second. Deepika used to put her hand up for everything. By September, she didn't put her hand up even for easy sums. Once I saw her whisper the right answer to herself, fifty-six, and then look down at her notebook. I don't know what goes on inside her head. I only know she writes 'I'm bad at maths' on her rough pages now, in very neat letters.

qa.q: What did Ma'am tell Deepika after the first maths test?
qa.a: Ma'am said, 'Deepika, you're weak in maths, beta. Just focus on neatness.'

qa.q: What does Deepika whispering 'fifty-six' and looking down suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she still knew answers but no longer felt it was worth raising her hand, as if she had accepted the label.

qa.q: How could Ma'am help Deepika start answering again?
qa.a: Ma'am could wait longer when Deepika starts to answer, ask her questions on purpose, and praise her correct answers, like fifty-six.

qa.q: How might Trisha feel watching Deepika change?
qa.a: Trisha seems worried and a bit sad, noticing small things and seeing the label written in neat letters on Deepika's rough pages.

grounding: A classmate watches a girl labelled weak at maths get skipped and hurried, stop raising her hand and begin to believe the label.

subtype: Labelled weak and living down to it [Receiver]
passage:
Monday: at the parent-teacher meeting, Ramesh Sir read the report card aloud: 'Jatin: weak in maths.' Jatin's mother nodded quietly. That afternoon in oral tables, Sir went down the row and jumped straight past Jatin to the next boy.
Following Monday: Sir asked, 'Seven eights?' Jatin knew it, fifty-six, he had practised with Nani. He half-lifted his hand. Sir was already looking at the front bench. 'Yes, Kunal?' Jatin put his hand back under the desk.
A month later: his cousin asked him to help with a sum. Jatin shook his head. 'Don't ask me. I'm the maths-weak one.' He said it lightly, like a joke. That evening he didn't open his maths notebook, even though there was homework. 'What's the point,' he said to nobody, and went outside to play.

qa.q: What did Ramesh Sir read from Jatin's report card?
qa.a: He read, 'Jatin: weak in maths.'

qa.q: How might Jatin have felt when he put his hand back under the desk?
qa.a: He probably felt ignored and discouraged, since he knew the answer but Sir was already looking at the front bench.

qa.q: What small change could Ramesh Sir make in class?
qa.a: Sir could include Jatin in oral tables and wait a moment for his half-raised hand, giving him the same chances as the front bench.

qa.q: How might Jatin's cousin see him saying 'I'm the maths-weak one'?
qa.a: The cousin might believe it too, not knowing Jatin practised with Nani and knew seven eights.

grounding: Over a month a boy labelled weak at maths is skipped and overlooked in class, stops raising his hand and begins to call himself the maths-weak one.
